document_summary: New Jersey DCA 'Truth in Renting' guide (part 1 of 3) summarizing state landlord-tenant law, covering lease, security deposit, discrimination and non-renewal rules for New Jersey. | Part 2 of the New Jersey DCA 'Truth in Renting' guide (official state publication) covering NJ statewide landlord-tenant rules, including rent control, rent increases, habitability and eviction. | Part 3 of the New Jersey DCA Truth-in-Renting guide, covering eviction procedure, the statutory grounds for eviction under the Anti-Eviction Statute, relocation assistance, foreclosure tenant protections and agency contacts; statewide NJ.

rules.title: NJ Security Deposit Law: cap of 1.5 months' rent
rules.requirement: A landlord may not collect a security deposit above one and one-half times one month's rent, and prepaid rent held as security (including last month's rent) counts toward that cap. Deposits must be held in trust in an interest-bearing account, with interest going to the tenant, and returned within 30 days after the tenancy ends.
rules.key_value: 1.5 months' rent maximum; annual increases limited to 10% of the current deposit
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to most residential rental properties, including mobile homes.
rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings (a tenant there may opt in 30 days after a written request to the landlord). The interest-account rules do not apply to seasonal rentals of not more than 125 consecutive days.
rules.quoted_span: The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ).
rules.extraction_notes: Secondary DCA guide summarizing the statute; no effective date is stated in this document. The guide also says a pet deposit combined with the regular deposit cannot exceed 1.5 months' rent, and that the landlord may require only the first month's rent in addition to the deposit (max 2.5 months' rent at lease inception). Return deadline: 30 days, with an itemized list of deductions sent by registered or certified mail.}},{

rules.title: Anti-Eviction Act: good cause required for lease non-renewal
rules.requirement: Landlords of covered residential rentals may not refuse to renew a written or oral lease unless they have good cause under the Anti-Eviction Act. The good causes are listed in the guide's Eviction section (not in this part).
rules.key_value: Good cause required to refuse renewal or evict; a lease term ending is not itself a ground
rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings (which have a separate section), motels or hotels, and transient or seasonal units.
rules.quoted_span: No landlord of residential rental properties except t hose in owner occupied two or three family dwellings, motels or hotels, transient, or seasonal units may fail to renew any lease, regardless of whether it is written or oral unless they have good cause not to renew the lease.
rules.extraction_notes: Only the non-renewal summary appears in this part; the list of causes and any relocation-assistance duties are in later parts of the guide. The guide cites the statute as 'N.J.S.A. 2A:18:61.3'. No effective date is stated in this document.

rules.title: NJ Law Against Discrimination: source of lawful income protected in rental housing
rules.requirement: The LAD prohibits discrimination in renting property and requires equal treatment regardless of protected characteristics, including source of lawful income. The guide notes a landlord may still refuse to rent for insufficient income or poor credit history.
rules.key_value: Source of lawful income may not be a basis for refusing to rent
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to all landlord-tenant relationships, subject to the exceptions listed.
rules.exemptions: Two-family owner-occupied dwellings, rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home, and residences planned exclusively for and occupied by one sex (e.g. YMCA, age-restricted housing), as pertains to familial status.
rules.quoted_span: The New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (LAD), N.J.S.A. 10:5-12(g) to -(h), prohibits discrimination when selling or renting property and requires equal treatment in the sale or rental of housing regardless of race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, marital status, civil union status, domestic partnership status, familial status, affectional or sexual orientation, gender  identity or expression, mental and physical disability, nationality, or source of lawful income.
rules.extraction_notes: Secondary summary of the LAD; no effective date stated in this document. The guide also says a landlord may refuse to rent for insufficient income, an overcrowded unit, or poor credit history.

rules.title: No statewide rent control (municipal option); rent increase notice and unconscionability standard
rules.requirement: New Jersey sets no statewide cap on rents, and municipalities may adopt their own rent control or leveling ordinances. A landlord may raise rent only by properly terminating the lease and offering a new one, and the increase must not be unconscionable and must comply with any local ordinance.
rules.key_value: No state rent cap; increases must not be unconscionable and must follow any municipal rent control ordinance
rules.coverage_conditions: Statewide; local rent control boards apply only where a municipality has adopted a rent control or leveling ordinance.
rules.exemptions: Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion of construction (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5); government-subsidized rents, HUD-owned/subsidized or HUD-insured developments, and NJHMFA-financed projects may also be exempt.
rules.interaction: State leaves rent regulation to municipalities; municipal ordinances (e.g. Jersey City, Hoboken, Newark) govern the allowable increases where they exist. State notice rules in the Anti-Eviction Act apply alongside local rules.
rules.quoted_span: The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents.
rules.extraction_notes: Secondary summary by the state agency (DCA Truth in Renting guide). No effective date stated in this document. Increase procedure: written notice terminating the old lease and offering a new lease at the increased rent.

rules.title: Anti-Eviction Act (good cause required)
rules.requirement: A residential landlord may not evict or refuse to renew a lease, written or oral, without good cause under the Anti-Eviction Act. Possession may be recovered only through consent or court process, and a Notice to Quit is required for all good-cause evictions except nonpayment of rent.
rules.key_value: Good cause required to evict or fail to renew a residential lease
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to most residential rental properties, including single-family homes, mobile homes and mobile home park land, apartment buildings and complexes, and rooming and boarding homes (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-53 to -84).
rules.exemptions: May not apply to owner-occupied premises with two (2) or fewer rental units; does not apply to hotel or motel guests or guest houses rented to transient or seasonal tenants (except continual-residence occupants with no alternate residence); does not apply to a unit held in trust for a developmentally disabled immediate family member who permanently occupies it.
rules.interaction: Statewide rule; applies regardless of local rent control. Self-help evictions and lockouts are illegal.
rules.quoted_span: No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.
rules.extraction_notes: Effective date not stated in this document. Relocation-assistance duties are not addressed in this part of the guide. Summary of the statute found in the official DCA guide.

rules.title: NJ Anti-Eviction Statute (statutory grounds for eviction)
rules.requirement: A landlord may evict only on one of the enumerated statutory grounds (e.g. nonpayment, disorderly conduct, property damage, lease breach, habitual late payment, landlord-occupancy, removal from the rental market, condominium conversion), after the required notices. Tenants evicted for an illegal occupancy under G(3) are owed relocation assistance equal to six times monthly rent.
rules.key_value: Eviction only for enumerated statutory causes; relocation assistance of 6 x monthly rent for illegal-occupancy evictions (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(g)(3))
rules.coverage_conditions: Rental dwelling units generally; tenants of public housing, rooming/boarding houses and senior/disabled protected tenancies have additional rules. Notice to Quit periods vary by cause (3 days to 3 years).
rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings fall under N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2, which allows a narrower list of grounds (holdover after lease expiry, nonpayment, disorderly conduct, willful damage, rule or lease violations).
rules.interaction: Municipal rent control and local ordinances may add limits. A rent-increase eviction must comply with municipal ordinances, including rent control. Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction; a 90-day notice to quit is required where the buyer will occupy the unit.
rules.quoted_span: Listed below are the statutory grounds for eviction as set forth in the Anti-Eviction Statute.
rules.extraction_notes: Secondary summary (DCA handbook, part 3 of 3) of statutory law. The document states no effective date for the statute, so effective_date is null. Also noted: the reprisal ban (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-10.10) and the 18% interest on unpaid relocation sums are folded into this record. The handbook says the Hudson County Tenant Protection Act of 1992 gives extra protected-tenancy rights.
